topics.h: Where is the furry cat hiding? Let us find her!
p: Top means the highest part. Bottom means the lowest part.
Above means higher than something. Below means lower.
Inside means within a box or room. Outside means not in it.
On means touching the top. Under means below it.

ex.q: A cat sits in a basket. The basket is under a table. Where is the cat?
st: The cat is in the basket.
So the cat is inside the basket.
The basket is under the table.
ex.a: Inside the basket, under the table

topics.rl: Shoes go under the bed. Books go inside the bag. The fan is on top, near the ceiling.

topics.h: Where do muddy shoes go when we come home? Let us think!
p: We keep shoes outside the room.
Garbage goes inside the dustbin.
In the ball game, a ball in the basket is IN. A ball that misses is OUT.
A bed and a fan are inside a room. Trees and clouds are outside.

ex.q: Kabir throws 3 balls. Two drop in the basket. One falls on the floor. Say IN or OUT for each.
st: Ball 1 is in the basket: IN.
Ball 2 is in the basket: IN.
Ball 3 is on the floor: OUT.

topics.rl: At home we leave shoes outside the door. A banana peel goes inside the dustbin.

topics.t: On the tree, under the tree
topics.h: Who sits on the tree and who rests under it? Let us look!
p: Birds sit on the branches of a tree.
A boy resting in the shade sits under the tree.
On a face, the eyebrows are above the eyes.
The nose is above the mouth. The smile is below the nose.

ex.q: Draw a face. Where do the eyebrows go? Where does the smile go?
st: Draw the nose in the middle.
The smile goes below the nose.
ex.a: Eyebrows above the eyes, smile below the nose

topics.rl: On a hot day, people rest under a big tree. Crows and sparrows sit on its branches.

topics.h: Our Tiranga waves high! Which colour is on top?
p: Our flag, the Tiranga, has three colours.
Saffron is at the top. White is in the middle. Green is at the bottom.
White is below saffron and above green.
The blue Ashoka Chakra is in the middle of the white band.
The flag is a rectangle. It has 4 corners and 4 sides.

ex.q: Which colour is just below saffron in our flag?
st: Just below it is the white band.

topics.rl: On 15 August and 26 January we see the Tiranga at school and on buildings.

topics.h: Meow! The furry cat is hiding. Can position words find her?
p: In our song, we look for a lost cat. We use position words.
A clue tells where a thing is: on, under, inside, behind, next to.
Follow the clue and look in that place.
Give clear clues so a friend can find a hidden thing.

ex.q: Clue: 'The cat is under the table, behind the basket.' Where should Meena look?
ex.a: Under the table, behind the basket

topics.rl: When Papa cannot find his keys, a clue like 'on the shelf' helps him find them fast.

topics.h: Is the ice cream cart near or far? Let us look!
p: Near means close to you. Far means a long way away.
Something near looks big. Something far looks small.
You have a left hand and a right hand.
In a row, we read from left to right.

ex.q: In the row 🍎 🍌 🍇, which fruit is in the middle? Which is on the left?
st: Start from the left: 🍎 is first.
🍌 is next. It is in the middle.
ex.a: 🍌 is in the middle. 🍎 is on the left.

topics.rl: We look left and right before we cross a road. The moon is far. Your bag is near.

topics.t: Chhuk chhuk train: before and after
topics.h: Chhuk chhuk! Our train is here. Who is in front?
p: The engine is at the front. The bogies come after it.
Before means in front of. After means behind it in the line.
Count the bogies after the engine one by one.
In a human train, each child holds the child in front.
From a train window we see fields, rivers and bridges go by.

ex.q: 🚂 🟦 🟥 🟩 🟨. How many bogies come before the 🟥 bogie?

topics.rl: On a train trip, our coach number tells us if we are near the engine or at the back.

topics.h: Suwali spilled her buttons! How can she tidy them?
p: Sorting means putting things that are alike in one group.
Suwali sorts buttons by colour: red ones together, blue ones together.
Sorted groups are easy to count.
We can sort leaves, pebbles and buttons too.

ex.q: Buttons: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔴. Sort them by colour. How many are in each group?

topics.rl: At home we sort clothes, spoons and socks. Shopkeepers sort fruits into baskets.

topics.t: Sort another way, match one to one
topics.h: Can the same buttons be sorted in a brand new way? Yes!
p: The same buttons can be sorted again in a new way.
Sort by size: big buttons and small buttons.
Sort by holes: buttons with 2 holes and buttons with 4 holes.
Match one to one: give each cup one saucer.
If nothing is left over, both have the same number.

ex.q: 4 buttons: big red, small red, big blue, small blue. Sort them by size.

topics.rl: At lunch, we give each child one plate. If plates are left over, there are more plates than children.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.h: A snake and a worm went for a walk. Who is longer?
p: Long things stretch a big way from end to end.
Short things stretch only a little way.
To compare, put both ends at the same start line.
Longest means more long than all others. Shortest means less long than all.

ex.q: Riya has a pencil and a crayon. Both start at the same line. The pencil ends farther. Which is longer?
st: Line up one end of both.

topics.rl: A train is long. A toffee is short. A plait can be long or short.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.h: A ball and a plate are at a party. Which can bounce away?
p: Round things have curved sides, like a ball.
Flat things have flat faces, like a book.
A ball is round all over. It has no flat face.
Some things have both, like a tin can. Its sides are curved. Its top is flat.

ex.q: Is a dice round or flat?
st: All its faces are flat squares.

topics.rl: A laddoo and a ball are round. A book and a carrom board are flat.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.t: Round things, long things, box shapes
topics.h: A bangle and a ladder are very different. Can you tell how?
p: Round things like a bangle or a coin go in the circle box.
Long things like a pencil or a ladder go in the long rectangle box.
A matchbox has flat faces and corners. A brick and a lunch box have the same shape.
Things with the same shape match, even if size or colour is different.

ex.q: Which one has the same shape as a matchbox: a brick, a ball or a birthday cap?
st: A matchbox has flat faces and corners.
A brick also has flat faces and corners.
A ball is round. A cap is pointy.

topics.rl: A lunch box, a shoe box and a brick all have the matchbox shape.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.h: Let us build a house, a tower and a robot with things from home!
p: We can build with boxes, books, bottles, caps and funnels.
Boxes and books have flat faces. They stack well.
Balls are round all over. They roll off a stack.
A cone or a cap sits well on top, like a roof.
Tell the shapes you used: 'I used two boxes and a cap.'

ex.q: Aisha builds a tower: a big box, a small box and a cone on top. Why does it stand?
st: Boxes have flat faces. One sits flat on the other.
The cone has a flat bottom, so it sits on the box.
Its pointy top must go last.
ex.a: Flat faces stack, and the cone goes on top

topics.rl: Builders use bricks with flat faces to make strong walls.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.h: Push a ball and push a book. What happens?
p: Round things can roll, like a ball or a bangle.
Things with flat faces slide when we push them.
A cylinder can roll on its side. It slides on its flat end.
A cube cannot roll. It can only slide.

ex.q: Can a tin of biscuits roll and slide?
st: Lay the tin on its curved side. Push. It rolls.
Stand it on its flat end. Push. It slides.
ex.a: Yes, it can roll and slide.

topics.rl: Wheels roll on the road. A cupboard slides when we push it.

topics.ch: What is Long? What is Round?
topics.h: Let us test! Push it and see: does it roll, slide or do both?
p: Write R if a thing rolls. Write S if it slides.
Some things do both. A bottle rolls on its side and slides on its bottom.
Test it: push it on the floor or let it go down a slope.
Tick ✓ what it can do. Cross ✗ what it cannot do.

ex.q: Test a bottle cap. Does it roll, slide or both?
st: Stand it on its round edge and push. It rolls.
Lay it flat and push. It slides.

topics.rl: On the playground, a ball rolls down the slide. You slide down it!

topics.h: One juicy mango, and friends keep coming! How many are eating now?
p: At the start, 1 parrot eats the mango.
Then 1 more friend comes. Now there are 2.
Each time one more joins, we say the next number.
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. At the end, 9 friends share the mango!

ex.q: 4 animals are eating a mango. 1 more squirrel joins. How many are eating now?
st: One more joins: say the next number after 4.

topics.rl: When friends join your game one by one, you count on: 3, 4, 5...

topics.h: Your fingers can show any number up to 10! Let us try.
p: Show 3 birds with 3 fingers: one finger for each bird.
Show the same number with dots: ● ● ●.
Small numbers of dots can be seen at a glance, without counting one by one.
Fingers, dots and birds match when the number is the same.

ex.q: 4 sparrows sit on a wire. Show it with fingers and with dots.
st: Hold up 1 finger for each sparrow: 4 fingers.

topics.rl: We hold up fingers to tell our age: 6 fingers for 6 years!

topics.h: It is drawing day! Does every child get a crayon box?
p: Give each child one thing. Draw a line from each child to one thing.
If things are left over, there are more things than children.
If some children get nothing, there are fewer things.
If all match with none left, the numbers are equal.

ex.q: 4 children and 3 drawing sheets. Give one sheet to each child. Are there enough?
st: Match each sheet to a child: 3 children get one.

topics.rl: At a birthday party, we check there is one plate for each guest.

topics.h: Riya has 5 mangoes. Arjun has 3. Who has more?
p: More means a bigger number of things.
Less (or fewer) means a smaller number.
Match them one to one. The side with extras has more.
When both match fully, they are the same (equal).

ex.q: Riya has 5 mangoes. Arjun has 3. Who has more? How many more?
st: Match one of Riya's with one of Arjun's.

topics.rl: At a party, we check who got more sweets! We pick the shorter queue at a shop.

topics.h: Nani brought a basket of mangoes! Let us count them.
p: Each number is one more than the number before it.
The last number we say tells how many.
We can write numbers as digits: 1, 2, 3.

ex.q: What number comes just after 6?

topics.rl: We count steps on stairs, buttons on a shirt, and candles on a cake.

topics.h: Let us write numbers, colour stars and draw fruits!
p: We write numbers with digits: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
Start a digit at the top and go down.
To colour 5 flowers: colour and count 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Then stop.
To draw 4 fruits: draw one and count, until you say 4.

ex.q: There are 8 stars. Colour 6 of them. How many stay white?
st: Count the white ones: 7, 8. That is 2.

topics.rl: We write numbers on house gates, bus numbers and cake candles.

topics.h: Kabir has a plate of laddoos. How many can he share?
p: Touch each thing once and say a number.
Do not skip any. Do not count any twice.
The last number you say is how many in all.
Zero (0) means none at all.

ex.q: Count: 🪔 🪔 🪔 🪔 🪔 🪔. How many diyas?

topics.rl: We count rotis at dinner, kids in a team and diyas at Diwali.

topics.h: Dot-to-dot! Join 1 to 9 and see what picture appears.
p: In dot-to-dot, start at 1. Go to 2, then 3, all the way to 9.
If we skip a dot, the picture goes wrong.
To arrange cards, find the smallest first. Then the next one.
Smallest to largest: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.

ex.q: Cards: 7, 2, 5. Put them from smallest to largest.

topics.rl: Page numbers in a book and seat numbers in a bus go in order.

topics.h: 5 mangoes and 3 mangoes. Together, how many? Let us join groups!
p: Two small groups can join to make a number.
🍎🍎🍎🍎🍎 and 🍎🍎🍎 make 8.
7 can be 3 and 4, or 5 and 2, or 6 and 1.
Split a number into two parts. Join the parts to get it back.

ex.q: Which two groups make 7: 4 umbrellas, 3 umbrellas or 5 umbrellas?

topics.rl: Laddoos in two boxes, or shoes on two racks, can be joined to find how many in all.

topics.h: Dotty Bug has spots on her back. How many? Let us count!
p: Count the dots on a bug to know its number.
We can make dot designs with seeds, pebbles, buttons or bindis.
Dots in a neat pattern, like 2 on top and 2 below, are quick to read.
The same number can look different: ●●●● in a line and ●● over ●● are both 4.

ex.q: Bug A has ● ● ● in a line. Bug B has ● on top and ● ● below. Who has more dots?

topics.rl: Rangoli dots, bindis on a card and seeds in a flower design all show numbers.

topics.h: Roll the dice! Colour the boxes! Who will win?
p: A dice has 6 faces with dots from 1 to 6.
⚀ is 1, ⚁ is 2, ⚂ is 3, ⚃ is 4, ⚄ is 5, ⚅ is 6.
Roll the dice and colour that many boxes.
The player with more coloured boxes wins.

ex.q: Riya rolls ⚃. Kabir rolls ⚁. Each colours that many boxes. Who has more?

topics.rl: We use a dice in Ludo and in Snakes and Ladders.

topics.h: All the birds flew away! How many are on the branch now?
p: Birds fly away from a branch one by one.
When all fly away, none are left.
None is zero. We write it as 0.
At night we see 0 suns. An empty box has 0 sweets.
0 comes just before 1.

ex.q: 3 birds sit on a branch. One flies away, then another, then the last. How many are left?

topics.rl: An empty water bottle has 0 water. A cricket team with no runs has a score of 0.

topics.t: Tenth birthday: strings and frames of 10
topics.h: Joseph turns 10 today! Let us count candles, diyas and beads.
p: Joseph's cake has 10 candles. The room has 10 diyas.
A bead string of 10: count the beads, then add more to reach 10.
A ten frame has 2 rows of 5 boxes. That is 10 boxes.
When every box has a button, the frame shows 10.

ex.q: A string has 6 beads. Draw more to make 10. How many more?

topics.rl: Many pencil packs hold 10 pencils. Some sweet boxes hold 10 laddoos, 2 rows of 5.

topics.h: Ten fingers, ten toes! Ten is a special number.
p: 10 comes just after 9.
Two numbers can join to make 10, like 6 and 4.
Your two hands have 10 fingers in all.
10 things make one group of ten.

ex.q: Arjun has 7 marbles. How many more does he need to make 10?

topics.rl: Ten fingers help us count. A packet of 10 pencils is one ten.

topics.h: Put a stick in a row of 10 beads. What two numbers do you get?
p: Put 10 beads in a row. A stick between them splits them into two parts.
Stick after 3 beads: 3 and 7. Stick after 6 beads: 6 and 4.
Partner finger game: you show some fingers, your friend shows the rest to make 10.
Every split still makes 10 in all.

ex.q: 10 marbles are split by a stick. The left side has 2. How many are on the right?

topics.rl: Sharing 10 toffees between two friends can be done in many ways.

topics.h: Bundle 10 sticks with a rubber band. That is one ten!
p: 10 ones make 1 ten.
13 is 1 ten and 3 ones.
In 16, the 1 shows the ten. The 6 shows the ones.
20 is 2 tens and 0 ones.

ex.q: Harpreet has 1 bundle of 10 sticks and 4 loose sticks. How many sticks?

topics.rl: Bundles of 10 sticks are quick to count. Pencils come in packs of 10. It makes counting fast.

topics.h: So many sweets! Circle ten first, then counting is easy.
p: To count many things, first circle a group of ten.
Then count on the rest: 11, 12, 13...
A full ten frame is 10. A second frame shows the extra ones.
1 full frame and 4 more dots show 14.

ex.q: There are 16 sweets. Circle 10. How many are outside the circle? What is the number?

topics.rl: Shopkeepers count coins and bananas in tens to count faster.

topics.h: After 10, the numbers keep going! Let us count to 20.
p: Each number is one more than the one before.
20 is two groups of ten.

ex.q: What number comes between 14 and 16?

topics.rl: Bus numbers, page numbers and house numbers use these numbers.

topics.t: Biggest, smallest and in order to 20
topics.h: Who has the tallest tower? Let us compare numbers up to 20!
p: The smallest number comes first when we count. The biggest comes last.
Biggest to smallest: 18, 15, 11, 6.
With same-size blocks, the tower with the most blocks is the tallest.
Dot-to-dot to 20: join 1, 2, 3, all the way to 20, in order.

ex.q: Find the biggest and the smallest: 14, 9, 17, 12.
st: Count up: 9 comes first, so 9 is the smallest.
17 comes last, so 17 is the biggest.

topics.rl: In a race, the child with the biggest score wins a prize.

topics.h: Two friends bring sweets to share. How many sweets now?
p: Adding means putting things together.
We use the plus sign + to add.
The equal sign = shows the answer.
Start with the bigger number. Count on the smaller one.

ex.q: Riya has 4 laddoos. Mummy gives her 3 more. How many now?

topics.rl: We add when friends join a game or more sweets come to the plate.

topics.t: Add and draw: family, fingers and toes
topics.h: How many fingers and toes do you have? More than you think!
p: To show 3 + 2, draw 3 balls. Then draw 2 more. Count them all.
Count your family and a friend's family to find how many in all.
We have 10 fingers on our hands and 10 toes on our feet.
10 fingers and 10 toes make 20 in all.

ex.q: Riya's family has 4 people. Aisha's family has 5. How many people in all?

topics.rl: When two families meet for a festival, we add to know how many plates to lay out.

topics.h: Roll, win and tick! Who will win the most rounds?
p: Two players roll a dice. The bigger number wins that round.
Put a tick ✓ on the scoreboard for each win.
At the end, count the ticks for each player.
The player with more ticks won more rounds.

ex.q: Riya has ✓✓✓✓. Kabir has ✓✓. Who won more rounds? By how many?

topics.rl: In cricket, the scoreboard shows runs. More runs means the team is ahead.

topics.h: Hop, hop, hop on the number strip! Where will you land?
p: Colour 3 beads red and 4 beads blue. Count all the beads: 7.
On a number strip, start at the first number.
Hop forward as many steps as the second number.
The number where you land is the sum.

ex.q: Hop to find 5 + 3.

topics.rl: Hopscotch on the school ground is like hopping on a number strip.

topics.h: Kabir and Meena add in different ways. Can both be right?
p: Kabir counts all: 1, 2, 3, and so on. Meena counts on from the bigger number. Both get the same sum.
3 + 4 and 4 + 3 are both 7. The order does not change the sum.
A number can be made from two parts: 6 is 2 + 4, 3 + 3 or 5 + 1.
Match each sum with its answer, then check.

ex.q: Find 2 + 6 in two ways.
st: Way 2: start at 6 and count on 2: 7, 8.

topics.rl: Some friends add on fingers, some on beads. The answer stays the same!

topics.h: Is it a plus story or a minus story? Let us find out!
p: More coming? Then add with +.
Some going away? Then take away with -.
Adding makes the number bigger (but adding 0 keeps it the same).
Taking away makes the number smaller (but taking away 0 keeps it the same).

ex.q: There are 4 cows. 3 more cows come. Add or take away?

topics.rl: Guests arriving means add. Sweets eaten means take away.

topics.t: Make an addition story; sum puzzle
topics.h: Open your bag! Can you make a story that adds?
p: An addition story has two groups that join.
'I have 3 books. I put 2 more in my bag. Now I have 5.'
Sum puzzle: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
To make every line add to 6, put 1, 2 and 3 once in each line.

ex.q: A puzzle line has 1 and 2 filled in. Which number goes in the empty box so the line makes 6?

topics.rl: At home: 'Mummy bought 4 apples and 2 bananas. That is 6 fruits.'

topics.h: Beep beep! At each stop, a child gets down. Who is left?
p: The school bus has 5 children. At each stop, 1 child gets down.
5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0: one fewer each time.
When nobody is left, there are 0 children.
Draw the things, cross out the ones taken away, count the rest. Write it: 5 - 2 = 3.

ex.q: 6 children are on the bus. 1 gets down at each of 2 stops. How many are left?

topics.rl: On the way home, the bus gets emptier at every stop.

topics.h: Five birds sit on a wire. Two fly away. How many stay?
p: Subtracting means taking away.
We use the minus sign - to take away.
Count back to find what is left.
Taking away 0 leaves the same number.

ex.q: Kabir has 8 grapes. He eats 3. How many are left?

topics.rl: When we eat sweets, the plate has fewer. When friends leave, fewer play.

topics.h: A hand covers some dots! How many are hiding?
p: A card has 7 dots. A hand hides some. We see 4.
Hidden = all the dots take away the dots we see: 7 - 4 = 3.
Check by adding: 4 seen + 3 hidden = 7.
Adding and taking away are linked: 4 + 3 = 7, so 7 - 3 = 4.

ex.q: 8 dots in all. 5 can be seen. How many are hidden?

topics.rl: If you know 10 children are in a group and 7 are in the room, 3 must be outside.

topics.h: Hop backwards on the number strip! Careful, little frog!
p: To find 9 - 3, start at 9 on the number strip.
Hop back 3: 8, 7, 6. Land on 6.
You can also count up from 3 to 9, or use your fingers.
Any way is fine if the answer is right. Check by adding: 6 + 3 = 9.

ex.q: Find 8 - 5 by hopping back.

topics.rl: Counting down for a rocket launch is like hopping back: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1!

topics.h: The farm has lots of vegetables! Let us add them up.
p: Start with the bigger number. Count on the smaller one.
Make 10 first. Then add what is left.
9 + 4: give 1 to 9 to make 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
Changing the order gives the same sum. 3 + 8 = 8 + 3.

ex.q: Meena picks 8 carrots and 5 more. How many carrots?

topics.rl: We add runs in cricket and coins in a piggy bank.

topics.t: Fill the blank: mala and hops
topics.h: Slide the beads on a mala and hop on the line to find big sums!
p: Fill the blank to finish a sum: 7 + 5 = ___ asks what 7 and 5 make.
A ginladi (bead mala) has beads in groups of 10. Slide beads to add.
On a number line, start at the first number and hop forward.
9 + 6: start at 9, hop 6, land on 15.

ex.q: Use a mala to find 8 + 7.
st: Slide 2 more to fill the ten. 5 are still to slide.

topics.rl: Counting beads on a mala or seeds in a row helps us add big numbers.

topics.h: Big numbers have a ten hiding inside! Use it to add fast.
p: 12 is 10 and 2. To add 12 + 6, first add the ones: 2 + 6 = 8.
There is often another way: count on 6 from 12: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18.
Talk with a friend. Both ways give the same answer.

ex.q: Find 13 + 5 by splitting 13.

topics.rl: ₹10 note and ₹3 in coins, plus ₹5 more: add the coins first, then the note.

topics.h: Picnic time! How much food should we pack?
p: Read the story and find the numbers.
'In all' and 'altogether' tell us to add.
For a picnic, list the food: 6 puris, 5 idlis, 4 bananas.
With three numbers, add two first. Then add the third.

ex.q: For a picnic: 6 puris and 8 sandwiches. How many things to eat?

topics.rl: Before a trip, Mummy counts the food so everyone gets enough.

topics.h: Rabbits nibbled some carrots! How many are left?
p: Count back to take away.
Or count up from the small number to the big one.
15 - 5 = 10. Take away the ones to reach 10.
Taking away makes the number smaller (unless we take away 0).

ex.q: There are 14 cabbages. 6 are sold. How many are left?

topics.rl: When sweets get eaten or toys get given away, we subtract.

topics.h: Draw a number strip on the floor. How many ways can you reach 12?
p: Draw a number strip from 0 to 20 on the floor with chalk.
Reach 12 in different ways: 10 + 2, 8 + 4, 15 - 3.
Many sums and take-aways can land on the same number.
Check each way by hopping it.

ex.q: Find two ways to reach 14 on the strip.

topics.rl: There are many roads to the same market. Numbers are like that too!

topics.h: Every farm has a story. Let us solve them!
p: Read the story slowly.
Find the numbers.
Words like 'more come', 'in all', 'altogether' usually mean add.
Words like 'left', 'gave away', 'ate' usually mean take away.

ex.q: Harpreet has 9 potatoes. Her dadi gives her 6 more. How many in all?
st: 'More' and 'in all' tell us to add.

topics.rl: At the sabzi market we count what we buy and what is left.

topics.t: Two-step stories: diyas and the bus
topics.h: Some stories have two parts. Solve one step, then the next!
p: Some stories have two steps. Do one step at a time.
Diyas: made 8, sold 5, made 6 more. 8 - 5 = 3. Then 3 + 6 = 9.
Bus: 10 children, 4 get on, 3 get off. 10 + 4 = 14. Then 14 - 3 = 11.
Getting on means add. Getting off means take away.

ex.q: A bus has 12 children. 5 get off. Then 2 get on. How many now?

topics.rl: Before Diwali, a potter makes diyas, sells some and makes more again.

topics.h: Lina's whole family has come home! Who is taller than whom?
p: Count each family member once.
Lina is taller than baby Tinu but shorter than Papa. Lina is in between.
If A is taller than B, then B is shorter than A.
Compare with your own family: who is taller than you?
Stand back to back on a flat floor to compare.

ex.q: Mummy is taller than Lina. Lina is taller than Tinu. Who is taller than Tinu but shorter than Mummy?
st: Mummy is the tallest of the three.

topics.rl: At school, we stand in a line from shortest to tallest for the assembly.

topics.h: Lina's family stands in a row for a photo. Who is the tallest?
p: Tall means high from feet to head.
Taller means more tall than another.
Tallest means more tall than everyone else.
Shortest means less tall than everyone else.
Stand on the same floor to compare heights.

ex.q: Papa is taller than Lina. Lina is taller than baby Tinu. Who is the tallest?
st: So Papa is taller than both.

topics.rl: We line up by height in the school assembly. A coconut tree is taller than a rose plant.

topics.h: Which is closer to your home: the shop or the school?
p: Near means close. Far means a long way off.
Nearer means more near. Nearest means the most near of all.
Farther means more far. Farthest means the most far of all.
Count steps: fewer steps away means nearer.

ex.q: The shop is 5 steps from Lina's house. The school is 20 steps. The bus stop is 12 steps. Which is nearest? Which is farthest?
ex.a: The shop is nearest, the school is farthest

topics.rl: We walk to a nearby shop, but take a bus to a faraway city.

topics.h: A tree trunk and a thread: one is thick, one is thin!
p: Line things up from the same starting end to compare lengths.
The one that goes farthest is the longest. The one that ends first is the shortest.
Thick means wide. Thin means narrow.
A tree trunk is thick. A thread is thin.

ex.q: A rope, a ribbon and a thread start at one end. The ribbon ends last. The thread ends first. Which is longest? Which is shortest?
st: They start at the same end, so it is fair.

topics.rl: A belan is thick, a needle is thin. Tailors pick thin thread for sewing.

topics.h: No ruler? No problem! Use your hands and feet.
p: A handspan is from thumb tip to little finger tip, spread wide.
We can measure a table in handspans.
We can measure a room in footsteps.
We can measure a book with paper clips or erasers.
Count how many fit from one end to the other.

ex.q: Kabir puts erasers in a line along his pencil box. 6 erasers fit. How long is it?

topics.rl: Mummy measures cloth with her arm. We count steps from class to the gate.

topics.t: Guess, choose a unit and measure
topics.h: Guess first! Then measure. Who will guess closest?
p: Measure your arm in handspans, from shoulder to fingertips.
A friend's arm may give a different count.
Use handspans for big things, like a table. Use finger widths for small things, like an eraser.
First guess how many. Then measure. Was your guess close?

ex.q: Riya guesses her desk is 5 handspans long. She measures 7. How many more than her guess?

topics.rl: Dadi guesses how much atta she needs, then checks with a cup.

topics.h: Papa and Lina measure the same mat. They get different answers! Why?
p: Big hands give a smaller count.
Small hands give a bigger count.
Papa's handspan is bigger than Lina's.
To compare, use the same thing to measure.

ex.q: Papa measures a table: 5 handspans. Lina measures it: 8 handspans. Why?
st: Papa's hand is bigger, so fewer fit.
Lina's hand is smaller, so more fit.
ex.a: Lina's hand is smaller, so she counts more.

topics.rl: Tailors use one measuring tape so everyone gets the same answer.

topics.h: A feather and a brick: which one pulls your hand down?
p: Heavy things are hard to lift. Light things are easy to lift.
Heavier means more heavy. Lighter means less heavy.
Hold one thing in each hand. The hand pulled down more has the heavier thing.
A big thing is not always heavier. A balloon is big but light.
We check our weight on a weighing machine, at home or at a clinic.

ex.q: Lina holds a brick in one hand and a feather in the other. Which is heavier?
st: The brick hand is pulled down.

topics.rl: At the market, vegetables are weighed on a scale.

topics.h: How many mugs fill a bucket? Let us count and splash!
p: Fill a bucket with mugs of water. Count the mugs.
A bucket that takes more mugs holds more.
Use the same cup to fill bottles. More cups means it holds more.
We need a lot of water for a bath and only a little to drink.

ex.q: Bucket A takes 8 mugs. Bucket B takes 5 mugs. Which holds more? By how many mugs?
st: 8 is more than 5, so Bucket A holds more.

topics.rl: Saving water: use a bucket for a bath instead of a running shower.

topics.h: Twenty is not the end! Let us count on to thirty.
p: We read 21 as twenty-one and 30 as thirty.
To count many neem leaves or flowers, make groups of ten first, then count on.

ex.q: Meena has 2 bunches of 10 flowers and 4 loose flowers. How many flowers?

topics.rl: A month has about 30 days. Look at the dates on a calendar!

topics.h: Counting big piles one by one is slow. Count in tens!
p: Each step adds one more ten.
3 tens is 30. 5 tens is 50.
Ten tens make 100!

ex.q: Joseph has 4 packets. Each packet has 10 toffees. How many toffees?

topics.rl: Shops pack biscuits and pencils in tens. ₹10 notes are counted in tens too.

topics.h: Every big number has a tens part and a ones part!
p: In 34, the 3 means 3 tens. The 4 means 4 ones.
3 tens and 4 ones make 30 + 4 = 34.
The left digit shows tens. The right digit shows ones.
45 and 54 are different numbers!

ex.q: Aisha has 5 bundles of ten sticks and 2 loose sticks. What number is this?

topics.rl: ₹10 notes and ₹1 coins show tens and ones. Three ₹10 notes and five ₹1 coins make ₹35.

topics.h: Fill frame after frame! How many dots make 50?
p: Ten frames show a number: 3 full frames and 4 more show 34.
5 full ten frames show 50.

ex.q: Show 42 with ten frames.
st: Put 2 dots in the next frame.

topics.rl: Egg trays and chocolate boxes are like ten frames.

topics.h: Clip, clip, clip! Can you put every card in the right spot on the string?
p: A ginladi is a string number line. We clip number cards on it in order.
Each card goes just after the number before it.
Card 25 goes between 24 and 26.
Read the cards from left to right: each one is 1 more.

ex.q: Cards 31 and 33 are clipped on the string. Where does card 32 go?

topics.rl: Seat numbers in a cinema hall or train coach go in order like a ginladi.

topics.t: Count to 50 and fill the chart
topics.h: A number chart is like a map of numbers! Find the missing ones.
p: To count up to 50 things, make tens first, then count the ones.
A number chart has rows of ten: 1 to 10, 11 to 20, 21 to 30, and so on.
Going right, each number is 1 more. Going down, each number is 10 more.
Use these rules to fill missing numbers.

ex.q: In a number chart, which number is just below 34?

topics.rl: Classroom roll numbers, house numbers and calendar dates follow this order.

topics.h: Dadi sews tiny mirrors on a dupatta. So many! How do we count them?
p: In 73, the 7 means 7 tens and the 3 means 3 ones.
To count a big collection, like mirrors on a dupatta, make groups of ten.
99 is the biggest 2-digit number. After 99 comes 100.

ex.q: Dadi sews mirrors in groups of 10. She makes 6 groups and 3 more mirrors. How many mirrors?

topics.rl: Mirror work is a craft from Gujarat and Rajasthan. Count the mirrors on a bag or a dupatta!

topics.h: Let us explore numbers all the way up to 99!
p: After 29 comes 30. After 39 comes 40.
To find the bigger number, look at the tens first.
If the tens are the same, look at the ones.
99 is the biggest 2-digit number.

ex.q: Which is bigger: 47 or 52?

topics.rl: House numbers, bus numbers and cricket scores go past 20.

topics.h: A long string with cards 1 to 99! Play with friends and put them in order.
p: Clip cards 1 to 99 on a long string. Friends take turns.
To order numbers, look at the tens first.
If the tens are the same, look at the ones.
Smallest to largest: 19, 45, 54, 91.

ex.q: Put 63, 36 and 60 in order, smallest first.
st: Tens: 6, 3, 6. 36 has the fewest tens, so it is smallest.
60 and 63 both have 6 tens. Ones: 0 is less than 3.

topics.rl: In a race list, runners are put in order of their numbers.

topics.h: Roll the dice, climb a ladder, slide down... reach 100 to win!
p: A board game has squares numbered 1 to 100, in rows of 10.
Roll a dice and move forward that many squares.
A ladder takes you up to a bigger number. A slide takes you back to a smaller one.
Fill missing squares by counting on from the number before.

ex.q: Riya is on 34. She rolls ⚄. Where does she land?

topics.rl: Snakes and Ladders (Moksha Patam) is an old Indian board game.

topics.h: Circles, triangles and lines make dancing people! Welcome to Warli art.
p: Warli is a folk art from Maharashtra.
Warli pictures use circles, triangles and lines, in white on a brown wall.
A person has a circle head, a body of two triangles and line arms and legs.
We can count the houses, people and trees in a Warli picture.
For many tiny lines, guess first. Then count to check.

ex.q: A Warli picture has 3 houses and 8 people dancing. How many houses and people in all?

topics.rl: Many Indian walls, bags and cushion covers have Warli designs. Look for them!

topics.h: Utsav time! Rangoli, flags and bead garlands all have patterns.
p: A pattern repeats again and again.
The part that repeats is the 'core'.
🔴🔵🔴🔵 repeats red, blue.
Patterns can use colours, shapes, sizes or sounds.

ex.q: Look: 🌼🌸🌼🌸🌼🌸. What part repeats?

topics.rl: Toran on doors, rangoli at Diwali and stripes on a kurta show patterns.

topics.h: Toran, flags and lights! Festivals are full of patterns.
p: At festivals we see patterns in flags, torans, garlands and lights.
A string of lights may go red, green, red, green.
To extend a pattern by colouring, find the core and colour it again and again.
A pattern keeps the same order every time.

ex.q: A toran has 🥭🌼🥭🌼 ___ ___. Colour the next two.

topics.rl: During Diwali, Pongal or Eid, look at the lights and paper flags. Can you spot the core?

topics.h: Patterns help us guess what comes next!
p: Find the part that repeats.
Say the pattern aloud.
Keep going in the same order.
Check by saying it again from the start.

ex.q: What comes next? 🔺🔵🔺🔵🔺 ___

topics.rl: Lights on a Diwali string blink in patterns. We can guess the next colour!

topics.h: Dip your thumb in paint and press! Let us print a pattern.
p: Dip your thumb in colour and press it on paper. That is a thumb print.
A finger print is smaller than a thumb print.
Make a pattern: thumb, finger, thumb, finger.
Fill your space with your own print pattern. Keep the same order.

ex.q: Aisha prints thumb, finger, thumb, finger. What comes next?

topics.rl: Thumb prints can make caterpillars, flowers and borders on greeting cards.

topics.h: Numbers can make patterns too!
p: 2, 4, 6, 8 goes up by 2 each time.
5, 10, 15, 20 goes up by 5 each time.
10, 9, 8, 7 goes down by 1 each time.
Find the jump, then keep going.

ex.q: What comes next? 3, 6, 9, ___

topics.rl: House numbers on one side of a road often go 2, 4, 6, 8.

topics.h: Doorsteps bloom with dots and lines! Let us make a kolam.
p: Kolam and rangoli are floor designs made at doorsteps.
A kolam is drawn with rice flour around a grid of dots.
Many kolams look the same on both sides, like butterfly wings.
To complete one, copy one side onto the other side.
Rangoli colours and shapes often repeat around the centre.

ex.q: A kolam has a grid of 3 rows of 3 dots. How many dots?

topics.rl: In many Indian homes, a kolam or rangoli is drawn at the door every morning or at festivals.

topics.h: Look around! Patterns hide on leaves, tiles, sarees and zebras.
p: Arrange pebbles, flowers, leaves, bangles, coins or caps in a pattern.
Nature has patterns: a beehive, butterfly wings, zebra stripes.
Sarees, curtains and floor tiles have repeating designs too.
Look for the part that repeats.

ex.q: Make a pattern with 2 caps and 1 coin. Show two cores.
st: The core is cap, cap, coin.
ex.a: cap, cap, coin, cap, cap, coin

topics.rl: Look at your school floor, your mother's saree border or a pineapple. Find the repeat!

topics.h: Clap, snap, stamp! Your body can make patterns too.
p: Cut out pictures of things with patterns, like tiles, cloth and leaves. Paste them on a sheet. That is a collage.
Patterns can be made with actions: clap, snap, stamp.
Clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap, stamp. The core is clap, clap, stamp.
Do the core again and again in the same order.

ex.q: Clap, snap, stamp, clap, snap, stamp. What comes next?
st: The core is clap, snap, stamp.

topics.rl: Garba and dandiya dancers repeat steps in a pattern. Music has beats that repeat too.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: Things in a day happen in order. What comes first?
p: First we wake up. Next we brush. Then we eat breakfast.
We use words like first, next, then and last.
Before means earlier. After means later.
Some things must happen before others.

ex.q: Put in order: eat breakfast, wake up, go to school.
ex.a: Wake up, eat breakfast, go to school

topics.rl: Making chai has an order: boil water, add tea leaves, add milk, then pour.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: Pihu has a busy day! Let us follow her from morning to night.
p: Morning: Pihu wakes up, exercises, brushes her teeth, takes a bath and eats breakfast.
Day: she goes to school, eats lunch with friends and rests.
Evening: she plays and does her homework.
Night: she eats dinner, reads a story and sleeps.

ex.q: Pihu brushes her teeth and eats breakfast. Which does she do first?
st: We brush our teeth soon after waking up.
Breakfast comes after brushing and bath.

topics.rl: Your day has a morning, a school time, an evening and a night too!

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: What do you do every single day? That is your routine!
p: A routine is what we do every day, in the same order.
We brush our teeth in the morning and again at night before bed.
Many of us bathe in the morning.
Tell your routine with words like first, then, after that and at night.

ex.q: Put Riya's morning in order: bath, wake up, breakfast, brush teeth.
ex.a: Wake up, brush teeth, bath, breakfast

topics.rl: A good routine keeps us healthy and on time for school.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: The sun rises, the sun sets. Our day has parts!
p: Morning: the sun comes up. We wake up and go to school.
Afternoon: the sun is high. We eat lunch.
Evening: the sun goes down. We play outside.
Night: it is dark. We see the moon and sleep.

ex.q: Riya sees the moon and stars. She goes to bed. What part of the day is it?
st: Moon and stars come out when it is dark.
We sleep when it is dark.

topics.rl: We say 'Good morning' when we wake up and 'Good night' before sleeping.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: Some jobs are quick. Some take a long time!
p: Blinking takes a very short time.
Brushing teeth takes a few minutes.
A school day takes many hours.
Growing a mango tree takes years!

ex.q: Which takes longer: drinking a glass of water or watching a cricket match?
st: Drinking water takes a few seconds.
A cricket match takes many hours.

topics.rl: A train trip to Nani's house takes longer than a walk to the shop.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: Hot sun, heavy rain, cold mornings! Why does the weather change?
p: India has seasons: summer, monsoon (rainy), winter and spring.
Summer is hot. We wear cotton clothes and use fans.
In the monsoon it rains a lot. We need umbrellas and raincoats.
Winter is cold. We wear sweaters. Spring brings new leaves and flowers.

ex.q: Riya takes her umbrella and raincoat to school. Which season is it?
st: Umbrellas and raincoats keep us dry.
We need them when it rains a lot.

topics.rl: In summer we drink cold lassi. In winter we eat hot gajar halwa.

topics.ch: How do I Spend my Day?
topics.h: Every season has its own food, clothes and festivals!
p: Write the season names: summer, monsoon, winter, spring.
Match a picture to its season: dark rain clouds go with the monsoon.
Foods we enjoy: mangoes and lassi in summer, hot soup and peanuts in winter.
Festivals come in seasons too: Holi in spring, Lohri and Pongal in winter.
Draw or paste your favourite season food and festival.

ex.q: People fly kites on Makar Sankranti in cold January. Which season is it?

topics.rl: Make a chart with four boxes, one for each season, and paste a food and a festival in each.

topics.h: Mummy puts laddoos on plates. Does every plate get the same?
p: Equal groups have the same number in each.
3 plates with 2 laddoos each are equal groups.
Count the groups. Count how many in one group.
Groups that are not the same are unequal.

ex.q: 4 plates. Each plate has 2 laddoos. Are the groups equal? How many laddoos?
st: Each plate has 2. So the groups are equal.

topics.rl: Pairs of socks, wheels on cars and fingers on hands come in equal groups.

topics.t: A visit to the amusement park
topics.h: Horse swings, a toy train and jalebis! Let us count at the mela.
p: Horse swing: each horse has 2 children. 4 horses: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.
Toy train: 3 bogies with 3 children each: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
Swings: 4 swings with 4 children each: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.
Jalebis: 6 plates with 3 on each. 3 added 6 times is 18. We say '6 times 3 is 18'.

ex.q: 6 plates with 3 jalebis on each. How many jalebis?
st: Skip count by 3, once for each plate.

topics.rl: At a mela, rides have seats in equal groups, so it is easy to count the riders.

topics.h: Off on a school trip! Two in every seat. How many in the bus?
p: A bus has 9 rows. 2 people sit in each row.
A crate holds 5 water bottles. 4 crates: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. That is 4 times 5.
Skip count to add fast: 5, 10, 15, 20.

ex.q: 4 crates of water. Each crate has 5 bottles. How many bottles?
st: Skip count by 5, once for each crate.

topics.rl: Shops get bottles, eggs and fruits in crates with the same number in each.

topics.h: '3 times 2' means 2, three times!
p: 3 times 2 means 3 groups of 2.
3 times 2 is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
2 times 5 is 5 + 5 = 10.
'Times' tells how many groups there are.

ex.q: Joseph hops 4 times. Each hop is 2 steps. How far does he go?

topics.rl: We clap 3 times, 2 claps each time. A shopkeeper puts 2 bananas in a bag, 4 times.

topics.h: Add the same number again and again. That is repeated addition!
p: 3 groups of 2 is 2 + 2 + 2.
We can skip count: 2, 4, 6.
4 groups of 5 is 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.

ex.q: Kabir has 3 packets. Each has 5 toffees. How many toffees?

topics.rl: A cricket team gets 2 runs, 2 runs, 2 runs. That is repeated addition!

topics.h: Cheenu goes shopping. Everything comes in packs!
p: Erasers come in packs of 2. 4 packs: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. 4 times 2 is 8.
Pencils come in packs of 3. 5 packs: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15. 5 times 3 is 15.
Apples come in bags of 3. 3 bags: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. 3 times 3 is 9.
Count the packs, then count the things in one pack.

ex.q: Cheenu buys 5 packs of pencils. Each pack has 3 pencils. How many pencils?
st: Skip count by 3, once for each pack.

topics.rl: Biscuits, soaps and pencils are sold in packs. Counting packs is faster!

topics.h: Let us go to the market! First, let us know our money.
p: Our money is the rupee. We write ₹.
Coins are round and made of metal: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10.
Notes are made of paper: ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100.
A ₹5 coin is worth five ₹1 coins.

ex.q: How many ₹1 coins make ₹5?

topics.rl: We pay with coins and notes at the sabzi market and the sweet shop.

topics.h: Rahim Kaka sells toys! Do you have enough money?
p: Rahim Kaka's toys have price tags: a whistle ₹5, a ball ₹10, a doll ₹14.
Four ₹5 coins make ₹20: 5, 10, 15, 20.
Two ₹10 notes make ₹20.
If a toy costs ₹14 and you have ₹10, you need ₹4 more.
With ₹30, pick toys whose prices add up to ₹30 or less.

ex.q: A doll costs ₹14. Sara has ₹10. How much more does she need?

topics.rl: At a mela, we check our money before choosing a toy.

topics.h: At the mela, toys have prices. Can we buy them?
p: The price tells how much a thing costs.
If we have enough money, we can buy it.
If we pay more, we get some money back. That is change.
Change = money given - price.

ex.q: A balloon costs ₹7. Riya pays ₹10. How much change?

topics.rl: At the sweet shop, the shopkeeper gives back change when we pay more.

topics.h: Arjun has a few coins. How much money does he have?
p: Add the value of each coin or note.
Start with the biggest one. Count on.
Different coins can make the same amount.

ex.q: Meena has a ₹10 coin, a ₹5 coin and a ₹2 coin. How much in all?

topics.rl: We count money in our piggy bank. Shopkeepers count the money we give.

topics.h: Can 1 coin do the work of 5 coins? Yes! Let us see how.
p: ₹10 can be one ₹10 coin, two ₹5 coins or five ₹2 coins.
To use the fewest coins, start with the biggest coin that fits.
₹7 with the fewest coins: ₹5 + ₹2. That is 2 coins.
Two groups match if they have the same total, even with different coins.

ex.q: Make ₹8 with the fewest coins. You have ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 coins.
st: ₹10 is too big. Take ₹5. ₹3 is left.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers give change with the fewest coins so their coin box does not run out.

topics.h: Clink! Clink! Coins go into the piggy bank. Let us save!
p: Saving means keeping some money for later.
A piggy bank keeps our coins safe.
Add each coin you put in to know how much you have saved.
Saving a little every day adds up to a lot!

ex.q: Monday ₹5, Tuesday ₹2, Wednesday ₹2 go in the piggy bank. How much is saved?

topics.rl: Many children save coins for a book, a toy or a gift for someone they love.

topics.h: Kabir's toys are all mixed up! Let us sort them.
p: Sorting means putting things that are alike together.
We can sort by colour, shape, size or kind.
Each group shares something the same.
The same toys can be sorted in different ways.

ex.q: Sort: 🚗 🧸 🚌 🪁 🚲. Which toys move on wheels?

topics.rl: We sort clothes in a cupboard, spoons in a drawer and books on a shelf.

topics.h: After sorting, we can count each group!
p: Sort the things first.
Count each group.
Then we can see which group has the most.
We can also find how many in all.

ex.q: 🚗🚗🚗 🧸🧸 ⚽⚽⚽⚽. Which group has the most?

topics.rl: A teacher counts how many children bring tiffin and how many buy lunch.

topics.h: A picture graph shows counts with little pictures!
p: Each picture stands for one thing.
A row with more pictures means more things.
We count the pictures in each row.
We can see the most and the least quickly.

ex.q: Toys in class: Cars 🚗🚗🚗🚗, Balls ⚽⚽, Dolls 🪆🪆🪆. Which toy is the most?

topics.rl: Teachers make picture graphs of favourite fruits or how children come to school.

topics.h: So many flowers! How can we remember how many of each colour?
p: Count the flowers of each colour.
Make a mark | for each flower. Every 5 marks, start a new group.
Write the counts in a table: colour on one side, number on the other.
Use the table to say true or false: 'There are more red than yellow.'

ex.q: Red flowers: ||||. Yellow flowers: ||||| ||. Which colour has more? Write the counts.

topics.rl: Teachers keep a record of who is present with a tick for each child.

topics.h: Hide, look, remember! Can you find the hidden numbers?
p: Memory game: number cards are hidden under bowls. Look, remember, then say which card is where.
In a tricky picture, count slowly. Touch or mark each thing once.
For a stack of logs, count row by row.
A puzzle may hide the numbers 1 to 10. Tick each one as you find it.

ex.q: A stack of logs has 3 at the bottom, 2 in the middle and 1 on top. How many logs?
st: Count row by row: 3, then 2, then 1.

topics.rl: When we pack school bags, we count books carefully so nothing is left behind.

topics.t: Who am I? Mirror and matchstick numbers
topics.h: I am a number with a secret. Use the clues to find me!
p: 'Who am I?' riddles give clues: 'I come just after 19.' Answer: 20.
Clues can use tens and ones: 'I have 2 tens and 5 ones.' Answer: 25.
A mirror flips a number from left to right. 18 in a mirror shows the 8 on the left, flipped.
Numbers can be made with matchsticks, like on a digital clock. 1 needs 2 sticks. 8 needs 7 sticks.
Moving one stick can change a number: 6 can become 9.

ex.q: Who am I? I am between 34 and 36.

topics.rl: Digital clocks and lift buttons show numbers made of little lines, like matchsticks.

topics.h: One answer, many questions! Let us play with sums.
p: Equal sides puzzle: put 1 to 5 in two lines that share the middle box. Both lines must have the same sum.
With 5 in the middle: 1, 5, 4 and 2, 5, 3. Both make 10.
Many questions have the answer 8: 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 10 - 2.
17 can be made in many ways: 10 + 7, 9 + 8, 12 + 5.

ex.q: Two lines share the middle box with 3 in it. Line one is 1, 3, 5. Line two is 2, 3, ___. Use 1 to 5 once each.

topics.rl: There are many ways to share sweets so that two friends get the same.

topics.t: Take away again; magic cross; centre numbers
topics.h: Take away, take away, take away... until nothing is left!
p: How many times can 5 be taken from 25? 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 0. That is 5 times.
Magic cross: put 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 in a row and a column that share the centre box. Both must have the same total.
With 7 in the centre: row 5, 7, 9 and column 6, 7, 8. Both make 21.
Centre puzzle: the centre number comes from the numbers around it. Find the rule, like 'add them'.

ex.q: How many times can you take 5 away from 15?

topics.rl: Sharing 20 laddoos, 5 at a time, until the box is empty is taking away again and again.

topics.h: Pick 3 balls and add the numbers! Can you hit the target?
p: Ball game: balls have numbers 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8. Pick any 3 balls and add.
Highest score: pick the 3 biggest: 8 + 6 + 5 = 19.
Lowest score: pick the 3 smallest: 2 + 4 + 5 = 11.
Fruit puzzle: if 🍎 + 🍎 = 10, then each 🍎 stands for 5.

ex.q: Balls: 2, 4, 5, 6, 8. Pick 3 balls to make 12.

topics.rl: In a fair game, children add their scores to see who wins.

topics.h: No repeats allowed! Can you fill the grid?
p: Shape sudoku: each row and each column has every shape once.
In a 3 by 3 grid with 🔺 🟦 ⚪, each row has all three, with no repeats.
Look at what is already in the row and the column. Put in the missing one.
With 4 objects like 🍎 🍌 🍇 🥭, each row and column has all four.
There can be more than one way to fill a grid. Try another!

ex.q: Row: 🔺 🟦 ___. Each row has 🔺, 🟦 and ⚪ once. What goes in the gap?

topics.rl: Sudoku puzzles in newspapers use numbers instead of shapes.

topics.h: Stack, fit and match! Puzzles with shapes and patterns.
p: Glasses can be stacked like a pyramid: 1 on top, 2 below, 3 below that.
Each new row has 1 more glass than the row above.
A missing piece must match the shape of the gap and the pattern around it.
A shadow has the same outline as the object.

ex.q: A glass pyramid has rows of 1, 2 and 3 glasses. Add one more row below. How many glasses in the new row?
st: Each row has 1 more than the one above.
The last row has 3, so the new row has 4.

topics.rl: In the evening, your shadow has your shape, with arms, legs and head!

topics.h: ₹49 with as few coins and notes as possible. Can you crack it?
p: We have ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20 coins and notes.
Start with the biggest one that fits. Then the next biggest.

ex.q: Make ₹27 with the fewest coins and notes.

topics.rl: Cashiers give change using big notes first, so they hand over fewer pieces.

qa.q: Riya keeps her laddoos in a box. Where are the laddoos?
qa.e: She put them in the box. So they are inside it.

qa.q: Which part of a tree is at the top?
qa.e: Leaves are high up on the tree. Roots are at the bottom.

qa.q: Arjun's cat sleeps under his bed. Is the cat above or below the bed?
qa.e: Under means below. So the cat is below the bed.

qa.q: A kite flies high over the house. The kite is ___ the house.
qa.e: High over the house means above the house.

qa.q: Meena plays in the garden. Her mummy is in the kitchen. Who is outside the house?
qa.e: The garden is outside the house. The kitchen is inside.

qa.q: Kabir puts his bag on the chair. Where is the bag?
qa.e: On means resting on the top. So the bag is on top of the chair.

qa.q: Riya ate a toffee. Where should the wrapper go?
qa.e: Garbage goes inside the dustbin. That keeps our home clean.

qa.q: Joseph comes home from the park. His shoes are muddy. Where should they go?
qa.e: Muddy shoes stay outside the room so the room stays clean.

qa.q: Aisha throws a ball. It drops into the basket. What does she call out?
qa.e: The ball went inside the basket. So it is IN.

qa.q: Kabir's ball misses and falls on the grass. Is it IN or OUT?
qa.e: The ball is not inside the basket. So it is OUT.

qa.q: Which one is found inside a room?
qa.e: A bed is kept inside a room. Clouds and trees are outside.

qa.q: Which one is found outside the house?
qa.e: The road is outside the house. So the bus is outside.

qa.q: A parrot sits on a branch. Where is the parrot?
qa.e: A branch is part of the tree. So the parrot is on the tree.

qa.q: Harpreet sits in the cool shade below a neem tree. Where is he?
qa.e: Below the tree means under the tree.

qa.q: Where are your eyebrows?
qa.e: Eyebrows are just above the eyes.

qa.q: Riya draws a smile on a face. Where should it go?
qa.e: The mouth is below the nose. So the smile goes there.

qa.q: A cat sleeps in the shade. A crow sits on a branch. Who is under the tree?
qa.e: The cat is in the shade below the tree. The crow is on the tree.

qa.q: Where is your nose?
qa.e: The nose is below the eyes and above the mouth.

qa.q: How many colours are there in the bands of our flag?
qa.e: The bands are saffron, white and green. That is 3.

qa.q: Which colour is at the top of the Tiranga?
qa.e: Saffron is the top band.

qa.q: Which colour is at the bottom of the Tiranga?
qa.e: Green is the lowest band.

qa.q: Where is the Ashoka Chakra on the flag?
qa.e: The chakra is in the middle of the white band.

qa.q: The white band is below saffron. What is below the white band?
qa.e: Green is below white, at the bottom.

qa.q: Our flag is a rectangle. How many corners does it have?
qa.e: A rectangle has 4 corners, one at each end of the top and the bottom.

qa.q: Clue: The cat is inside the cupboard. Where will you look?
qa.e: Inside the cupboard means we open it and look in.

qa.q: Arjun hid his ball under the chair. Which clue is right?
qa.a: The ball is under the chair
qa.e: The ball is below the chair. So 'under the chair' is right.

qa.q: Which is the best clue?
qa.a: The pen is inside my pencil box
qa.e: It says the place and the position word. Easy to find!

qa.q: The cat sits on the wall. Riya looks under the bed. Will she find it?
qa.e: The cat is on the wall, not under the bed. Riya is looking in the wrong place.

qa.q: Kabir says, 'The toy is behind the TV.' Where should Aisha look?
qa.a: At the back of the TV
qa.e: Behind means at the back.

qa.q: In the song, children look for a lost cat. Which words help most?
qa.a: Position words like on and under
qa.e: On, under and inside tell where to look for the cat.

qa.q: Aisha stands next to her school bag. The bus stop is a long walk away. What is near Aisha?
qa.e: Next to her means close. So the bag is near.

qa.q: Which one is far from us?
qa.e: The sun is very, very far away. That is why it looks small.

qa.q: In the row ⭐ 🌙 ☀️, what is on the far left?
qa.e: Start at the left end of the row. ⭐ comes first.

qa.q: In the row 🥭 🍌 🍎 🍇, what is just right of 🍌?
qa.e: Find 🍌. Move one step right. You reach 🍎.

qa.q: Harpreet sees two trains. One looks big. One looks tiny. Which train is far?
qa.e: Far things look smaller. So the tiny-looking train is far.

qa.q: Five children stand in a line: Riya, Joseph, Meena, Kabir, Aisha. Who is in the middle?
qa.e: Two children are on each side of Meena. So Meena is in the middle.

qa.q: 🚂 🟦 🟦 🟦 🟦 🟦. How many bogies come after the engine?
qa.e: Count the bogies after the engine: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

qa.q: 🚂 🟩 🟩 🟥 🟩. How many bogies are before the 🟥 bogie?
qa.e: Between the engine and 🟥 there are 2 green bogies.

qa.q: 🚂 🟨 🟥 🟨 🟨 🟨. How many bogies are after the 🟥 bogie?
qa.e: After 🟥 come 🟨 🟨 🟨. That is 3.

qa.q: Meena, Joseph and Riya make a human train. Meena is in front, then Joseph, then Riya. Who is just after Meena?
qa.e: Joseph holds Meena from behind. He is just after her.

qa.q: 🚂 ⬜ 🟥 ⬜. Colour the bogie just before 🟥 green. Which one turns green?
qa.e: The bogie just before 🟥 is between the engine and 🟥.

qa.q: Kabir's train passes a bridge. After that it passes a field. What came before the field?
qa.e: He saw the bridge first, so the bridge came before the field.

qa.q: Suwali has 🔴🔵🔴🔴🔵. How many red buttons?
qa.e: Pick out the red ones: 🔴🔴🔴. That is 3.

qa.q: Which button goes in the blue group?
qa.e: Only 🔵 is blue.

qa.q: Why do we sort buttons into groups?
qa.e: When alike things are together, we can count each group fast.

qa.q: Riya sorts leaves: 🍃🍂🍃🍂🍂. How many green leaves 🍃?
qa.e: Pick out the green ones: 🍃🍃. That is 2.

qa.q: Joseph puts grey pebbles in one heap and white pebbles in another. How is he sorting?
qa.e: Grey and white are colours. So he sorts by colour.

qa.q: 🟡🟡🔵🟡🔵. Sort by colour. Which group has more?
qa.e: Yellow has 3. Blue has 2. Yellow has more.

qa.q: Buttons: big 🔵, small 🔵, big 🔴. Sort by size. How many big buttons?
qa.e: The big ones are big 🔵 and big 🔴. That is 2.

qa.q: Meena sorted buttons by colour. Now she sorts the same buttons by holes. Is that fine?
qa.a: Yes, we can sort in a new way
qa.e: The same things can be sorted in many ways.

qa.q: Which is a way to sort buttons?
qa.e: Buttons can have 2 or 4 holes. We can group them that way.

qa.q: There are 4 children and 4 chairs. Each child sits on one chair. How many chairs are left?
qa.e: Each chair got one child. None are left.

qa.q: 5 cups and 3 saucers. Put one saucer under each cup. How many cups get no saucer?
qa.e: 3 cups get saucers. 2 cups are left without one.

qa.q: Arjun has 3 friends and 3 pencils. He gives each friend one pencil. What is true?
qa.a: Same number of friends and pencils
qa.e: Every friend got one and none were left. So they are the same.

qa.q: Which is longer?
qa.e: A cricket bat is much longer than a tiny matchstick.

qa.q: Which is the shortest?
qa.e: A paper clip is the shortest of the three.

qa.q: Meena's ribbon is long. Aisha's ribbon is short. Whose ribbon is longer?
qa.e: Long is more than short. So Meena's ribbon is longer.

qa.q: Two sticks start at the same line. Stick A ends first. Which is shorter?
qa.e: The stick that ends first does not go as far. So Stick A is shorter.

qa.q: Which animal has a long trunk?
qa.e: Only the elephant has a trunk. It is long!

qa.q: Kabir lays a pen next to a ruler. The ruler is longer. Which is shorter?
qa.e: If the ruler is longer, the pen must be shorter.

qa.q: Which one is round all over?
qa.e: A ball is curved everywhere. Books and bricks have flat faces.

qa.q: Which one has flat faces?
qa.e: A dice has 6 flat faces. Oranges and marbles are round.

qa.q: A square gift box is shaped like a ___.
qa.e: A box with square faces is like a cube.

qa.q: A sheet of paper is flat. Which is also flat?
qa.e: A notebook cover is flat like the paper. A laddoo and a ball are round.

qa.q: A tin of ghee has curved sides. What shape is it like?
qa.e: A tin has a curved side and two flat round ends. That is a cylinder.

qa.q: Joseph's birthday cap is pointy at the top. It is like a ___.
qa.e: A birthday cap has a round bottom and a point on top. That is a cone.

qa.q: Which thing has the same shape as a matchbox?
qa.e: A brick has flat faces and corners, just like a matchbox.

qa.q: Riya draws a bangle. Which box should it go in?
qa.e: A bangle is round. Round things go in the circle box.

qa.q: Kabir draws a ladder. Which box should it go in?
qa.e: A ladder is long. Long things go in the rectangle box.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT shaped like a box?
qa.e: A ball is round all over. A brick and a matchbox are box shapes.

qa.q: Meena has a small ball and a big football. Do they have the same shape?
qa.a: Yes, both are round like a ball
qa.e: Size does not change shape. Both are round all over.

qa.q: How many flat faces does a matchbox have?
qa.e: Top, bottom and 4 sides. That is 6 faces.

qa.q: Joseph wants a tall tower. Which is best to stack?
qa.e: Boxes have flat faces. They sit on each other without rolling.

qa.q: Why does a ball fall off a stack?
qa.e: A ball has no flat face to sit on, so it rolls off.

qa.q: Riya makes a toy house from a box. What can be its roof?
qa.e: A cone has a flat bottom and a pointy top, like a roof.

qa.q: Kabir makes a bus from a box. Which can be its wheels?
qa.e: Bottle caps are round like wheels.

qa.q: Meena stacks 3 books. She puts 1 box on top. How many things are in her stack?
qa.e: 3 books and 1 box make 4 things.

qa.q: Aisha says, 'My robot has a box for a body and two glasses for legs.' What is she doing?
qa.e: She names the shapes in her model.

qa.q: Which one rolls?
qa.e: A marble is round. Round things roll.

qa.q: Which one will slide, not roll?
qa.e: A box has flat faces. It slides.

qa.q: Why can a bicycle wheel roll?
qa.e: Round things roll. A wheel is round.

qa.q: Arjun pushes a cube. What does it do?
qa.e: A cube has flat faces. It slides.

qa.q: Which can roll on one side and slide on another?
qa.e: A tin rolls on its curved side. It slides on its flat end.

qa.q: Aisha wants a toy that rolls down a slide. Which should she pick?
qa.e: A ball is round, so it rolls down.

qa.q: Riya writes R or S. What should she write for a football?
qa.e: A football rolls. R means rolls.

qa.q: What should Riya write for a brick?
qa.e: A brick has flat faces. It slides, so S.

qa.q: Which can roll and slide both?
qa.e: A bottle rolls on its curved side and slides on its flat bottom.

qa.q: Kabir pushes an eraser on the floor. What does it do?
qa.e: An eraser has flat faces. It slides.

qa.q: Joseph tests: ball rolls ✓, book ✗, glass rolls ✓, box ✗. How many things can roll?
qa.e: Ball and glass got a tick. That is 2.

qa.q: A tin can rolls on its side. Can it also slide?
qa.e: Stand it on its flat end and push. It slides.

qa.q: A parrot is eating a mango all alone. How many are eating?
qa.e: Just one parrot is eating. That is 1.

qa.q: 3 squirrels are eating. 1 more joins. How many now?
qa.e: 1 more than 3 is 4.

qa.q: What is 1 more than 6?
qa.e: After 6 comes 7.

qa.q: 7 birds share a mango. 1 more comes. Then 1 more comes. How many now?
qa.e: 7, then 8, then 9.

qa.q: Friends join one by one. Count on: 5, 6, 7, ___, 9.
qa.e: After 7 comes 8, then 9.

qa.q: Count the mango eaters: 🐦🐦🐦🐦🐦🐦🐦🐦🐦. How many in all?
qa.e: Touch each bird once: 1 to 9.

qa.q: 🐦🐦🐦 How many fingers will you show for these birds?
qa.e: One finger for each bird. 3 birds, 3 fingers.

qa.q: Riya shows 5 fingers. How many dots should she draw?
qa.e: One dot for each finger. 5 fingers, 5 dots.

qa.q: Kabir draws ● ● ● ● ● ● ●. How many fingers match?
qa.e: Count the dots: 1 to 7. Show 7 fingers.

qa.q: Which dot card matches 2 fingers?
qa.e: 2 fingers need 2 dots.

qa.q: Joseph holds up a whole hand and 1 more finger. How many dots match?
qa.e: A whole hand is 5. One more is 6.

qa.q: Which dot card shows the same number as 4 birds?
qa.e: 4 birds need 4 dots, one for each.

qa.q: 5 children and 5 brushes. One brush each. How many brushes are left?
qa.e: Each child got one. No brush is left.

qa.q: 4 children and 6 crayons. One crayon each. What is true?
qa.e: After each child gets one, 2 crayons are left. So more crayons.

qa.q: ☕☕☕ 🥄🥄🥄🥄🥄. Which group has fewer?
qa.e: 3 cups, 5 spoons. 3 is fewer than 5.

qa.q: 6 children and 4 sheets. How many children do not get a sheet?
qa.e: 4 children get sheets. 2 children are left without.

qa.q: ☕☕☕☕ 🥄🥄. Circle the group with fewer items.
qa.e: 2 spoons and 4 cups. Spoons are fewer.

qa.q: 3 children each get one pencil. 2 pencils are left. How many pencils were there?
qa.e: 3 given out and 2 left. 3 + 2 = 5.

qa.q: Which is more?
qa.e: 9 comes after 6 when we count. So 9 is more.

qa.q: Which is the least?
qa.e: 2 comes first when we count. It is the smallest.

qa.q: Aisha has 🍬🍬🍬🍬. Joseph has 🍬🍬. Who has fewer sweets?
qa.e: Joseph has 2. Aisha has 4. 2 is less than 4.

qa.q: Kabir has 5 kites. Harpreet has 3 kites. How many more does Kabir have?
qa.e: Match 3 kites each. Kabir has 2 extra.

qa.q: Which is one more than 6?
qa.e: One more than 6 is the next number: 7.

qa.q: Meena has 4 bangles. Riya has 4 bangles. What is true?
qa.e: Both have 4. So they have the same number.

qa.q: What comes just after 4?
qa.e: Count 1, 2, 3, 4. Next is 5.

qa.q: What comes just before 9?
qa.e: Count 7, 8, 9. Just before 9 is 8.

qa.q: Which number is between 6 and 8?
qa.e: 6, 7, 8. The number in between is 7.

qa.q: How do we write 'three' as a number?
qa.e: Three is written as 3.

qa.q: Count: 2, 3, 4, ___, 6. What is missing?
qa.e: After 4 comes 5. Then 6.

qa.q: There are 9 steps. Riya has climbed 8. How many more steps to the top?
qa.e: From 8, one more step makes 9.

qa.q: How do we write the number 'six'?
qa.e: Six is written as 6.

qa.q: Riya must colour 5 of these flowers: 🌸🌸🌸🌸🌸🌸🌸. How many stay uncoloured?
qa.e: 7 flowers, 5 coloured. 6, 7 are left: 2.

qa.q: Kabir drew 🍌🍌🍌. He must draw 4 fruits. How many more should he draw?
qa.e: He has 3. One more makes 4.

qa.q: Aisha has to colour 8 stars. Which shows 8?
qa.e: Count each row. Only the first one has 8.

qa.q: Joseph has to colour 6 balls. He has coloured 4. How many more?
qa.e: 4, then 5, 6. That is 2 more.

qa.q: Meena writes how many fingers are on one hand. What does she write?
qa.e: One hand has 5 fingers.

qa.q: How many mangoes? 🥭🥭🥭🥭🥭
qa.e: Touch and count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

qa.q: How many diyas? 🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔
qa.e: Count each diya once: 1 to 7.

qa.q: Arjun has no balloons. How many balloons does he have?
qa.e: No balloons means zero. We write 0.

qa.q: How many stars? ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Meena counts 1, 2, 3, 4 laddoos. How many laddoos are there?
qa.e: The last number she said is 4. So there are 4.

qa.q: How many footballs? 🏏 ⚽ ⚽ ⚽
qa.e: 🏏 is a bat, not a ball. Count only the footballs: 3.

qa.q: In a dot-to-dot, you are at dot 4. Which dot is next?
qa.e: After 4 comes 5.

qa.q: Cards 6, 1, 3. Which is the smallest?
qa.e: 1 comes first when we count.

qa.q: Put 8, 4, 6 from smallest to largest. Which card is in the middle?
qa.e: In order: 4, 6, 8. 6 is in the middle.

qa.q: Which is in order from smallest to largest?
qa.e: 2 is less than 5, and 5 is less than 9.

qa.q: Riya joins dots 1, 2, 3, 5. Which dot did she miss?
qa.e: After 3 comes 4, then 5.

qa.q: Cards 9, 7, 8. Smallest to largest, which card goes last?
qa.e: In order: 7, 8, 9. 9 is last.

qa.q: 🍎🍎🍎🍎🍎 and 🍎🍎🍎. How many fruits in all?
qa.e: 5 and 3 make 8.

qa.q: Which two groups make 7 umbrellas?
qa.e: 4 and 3 make 7. The others make 8.

qa.q: Riya splits 6 beads into two parts. One part has 2. How many in the other?
qa.e: 2 and 4 make 6.

qa.q: Which is NOT a way to make 5?
qa.e: 3 and 3 make 6, not 5.

qa.q: 9 is 5 and ___.
qa.e: 5 and 4 make 9.

qa.q: Kabir has 8 marbles in two pockets. One pocket has all 8. How many in the other?
qa.e: 8 and 0 make 8. The other pocket is empty.

qa.q: Dotty Bug has ●●●●●● on her back. How many dots?
qa.e: Count each dot once: 1 to 6.

qa.q: Riya makes a design with 3 bindis on top and 2 below. How many bindis?
qa.e: 3 and 2 make 5.

qa.q: Which shows the same number as ●●●●?
qa.e: 2 and 2 make 4. It just looks different.

qa.q: Kabir uses 7 seeds for a flower design. He adds 1 seed in the middle. How many seeds now?
qa.e: 1 more than 7 is 8.

qa.q: Bug A: ● ● ●. Bug B: ●● and ●. What is true?
qa.e: Bug A has 3. Bug B has 2 and 1, which is 3.

qa.q: Aisha makes 2 rows of buttons with 4 in each row. How many buttons?
qa.e: 4 and 4 make 8.

qa.q: Arjun rolls ⚄. How many boxes does he colour?
qa.e: ⚄ has 5 dots. He colours 5 boxes.

qa.q: Which dice face shows 3?
qa.e: ⚂ has 3 dots.

qa.q: Meena rolls ⚅. Joseph rolls ⚃. Who colours more boxes?
qa.e: ⚅ is 6 and ⚃ is 4. 6 is more.

qa.q: What is the most dots on one face of a dice?
qa.e: The faces go from 1 to 6. The most is 6.

qa.q: Aisha rolls ⚁ and then ⚂. How many boxes does she colour in all?
qa.e: 2 and 3 make 5.

qa.q: Kabir coloured 4 boxes. Riya coloured 4 boxes. Who wins?
qa.e: Both have 4. Equal means a tie.

qa.q: 4 birds sit on a branch. All 4 fly away. How many are left?
qa.e: All flew away, so none are left. That is 0.

qa.q: How many suns can you see in the sky at night?
qa.e: The sun is not in the sky at night. So 0.

qa.q: Riya's lunch box is empty. How many idlis are in it?
qa.e: Empty means no idlis. That is 0.

qa.q: Which number comes just before 1?
qa.e: Counting back from 1 gives 0.

qa.q: 3 birds on a branch. 1 flies away. How many are left?
qa.e: 3 take away 1 is 2.

qa.q: Which is the least: 3, 0 or 1?
qa.e: 0 means none. It is less than any other count.

qa.q: Joseph's cake has 10 candles. 7 are lit. How many are not lit?
qa.e: 7 and 3 make 10. So 3 are not lit.

qa.q: A ten frame has 2 rows of 5 boxes. How many boxes in all?
qa.e: 5 and 5 make 10.

qa.q: A ten frame has 8 buttons. How many boxes are empty?
qa.e: 8 and 2 make 10.

qa.q: Riya's bead string has 5 beads. She wants 10. How many more?
qa.e: 5 and 5 make 10.

qa.q: A ten frame has just 1 empty box. What number does it show?
qa.e: 10 boxes with 1 empty means 9 buttons.

qa.q: Count the diyas at the party: 🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔🪔. How many?
qa.e: Count each diya once: 1 to 10.

qa.q: How many fingers on two hands?
qa.e: 5 on one hand and 5 on the other. 5 and 5 make 10.

qa.q: 8 laddoos are on a plate. How many more make 10?
qa.e: Count on from 8: 9, 10. That is 2 more.

qa.q: What comes just after 9?
qa.e: After 9 comes 10.

qa.q: 4 and ___ make 10.
qa.e: Count on from 4: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. That is 6.

qa.q: Riya has 5 red bangles and 5 green bangles. How many in all?
qa.e: 5 and 5 make 10.

qa.q: A box holds 10 pencils. It has 3. How many more fit?
qa.e: Count on from 3 to 10: that is 7 more.

qa.q: Partner game: Meena shows 4 fingers. How many must Arjun show to make 10?
qa.e: 4 and 6 make 10.

qa.q: 10 beads in a row. A stick goes after the 3rd bead. How many beads are after the stick?
qa.e: 3 and 7 make 10.

qa.q: Which pair splits 10?
qa.e: 6 and 4 make 10. The others make 9.

qa.q: Riya splits 10 shells. The left part has 5. How many in the right part?
qa.e: 5 and 5 make 10.

qa.q: Joseph shows 8 fingers. His friend shows 2. How many fingers in all?
qa.e: 8 and 2 make 10.

qa.q: 10 beads. The stick is after the 9th bead. How many beads are after it?
qa.e: 9 and 1 make 10.

qa.q: 1 ten and 6 ones make ___.
qa.e: 1 ten is 10. 10 and 6 make 16.

qa.q: How many ones are in 13?
qa.e: 13 is 1 ten and 3 ones.

qa.q: How many tens are in 20?
qa.e: 10 and 10 make 20. That is 2 tens.

qa.q: Kabir has 10 laddoos in a box and 5 loose. How many laddoos?
qa.e: 10 and 5 make 15.

qa.q: Which number has 1 ten and 9 ones?
qa.e: 1 ten is 10. 10 and 9 make 19.

qa.q: Meena has 17 beads. She makes a group of 10. How many beads are left over?
qa.e: 17 is 1 ten and 7 ones. 7 beads are left over.

qa.q: Count the flowers: 🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼🌼
qa.e: Circle 10, then count on 11, 12, 13.

qa.q: One full ten frame and 5 more dots. What number is it?
qa.e: 10 and 5 make 15.
